findings.title: Tick atomicity and state buffering are asserted, not designed
findings.description:
"Tick as transaction" (line 39) promises read, compute, commit. Step 4 (line 64) says the server "applies the updated entity state as the new canonical state," and the behavior engine doc (100-arch line 68) says the engine "returns the updated state array." The document never says whether the engine writes into the server's live arrays or a second buffer. Three consequences follow:

- **Partial state on failure.** If the arrays are updated in place, an exception mid-tick (shape mismatch, bad index, bad profile) leaves canonical state half-updated. The document has no tick-failure policy: skip, roll back, or halt.
- **Silent NaN.** Coincident agents produce zero-distance divisions. NumPy emits a `RuntimeWarning` by default and continues, so NaN enters canonical state, client snapshots, and logs. The "no silent failures" principle (line 45) has no validation step at commit to enforce it.
- **Thread upgrade breaks reads.** The thread-offload path (line 78) removes a guarantee the design currently gets for free. Serialization in step 5 reads a consistent snapshot only because tick and I/O run sequentially on one thread. Moving the tick to a thread makes those reads race with writes unless the design double-buffers or copies at commit. The document does not say this.

Required: specify the buffer model (write to B, swap on commit), the failure policy, and a commit-time validation check.

findings.title: The replay guarantee is asserted without its preconditions
findings.description:
Lines 74 and 90 claim that "given a log and the same configuration, the simulation can be reconstructed tick-by-tick." The document does not make the decisions this requires:

- **Canonical state is not inventoried.** Replay needs the tick counter, every RNG state, the next entity-ID counter, any free-list or compaction state, the seasonal state, and the profile registry. Line 80 lists only the entity arrays.
- **Randomness has no owner.** Disaggregation "spawned from the statistical model" (line 104) draws random numbers, and flocking jitter is common. The engine is "stateless between ticks" (100-arch line 70), so RNG state must be threaded through the tick function explicitly. Nothing says so.
- **Regenerated environments are not reproducible.** Line 72 says the environment is "generated or loaded... from configuration and seeds." NumPy's RNG policy (NEP 19) does not guarantee that `Generator` streams stay identical across releases. A log replayed after a NumPy upgrade would regenerate different terrain. Logs must either store generated environment data or pin library versions in the header.
- **Floating-point scope is unstated.** Replay on one platform and build may be achievable. Cross-machine or threaded-reduction replay is not guaranteed. The document should say which it requires.
- **Wall-clock input.** Step 1 (line 61) records a wall-clock timestamp. If season or day/night logic reads it, replay diverges. Simulated time should derive from the tick count.
- **Log content contradicts the engine design.** Line 74 logs "significant behavioral transitions," but the engine is "forces, not decisions" with no state machine (100-arch line 41), so there are no transitions to log. Line 90 lists "configuration changes" as replay inputs, but configuration loads only at startup (line 47).
- **Deferred choice.** Line 90 leaves snapshot-versus-event logging open ("depends on actual usage patterns"). That decision is the logging slice's first input.

Required: a replay-contract section with a canonical-state inventory, RNG ownership, a stated precision and platform scope, and a determinism test (run twice, compare state hashes) as the acceptance criterion.

findings.title: Entity lifecycle and the aggregation extension point are claimed but not designed
findings.description:
Line 112 calls the aggregation and variable-rate design "the key architectural decision now," but no decision appears anywhere in the document.

- The entity model (line 80) is positions, velocities, and profile indices. It has no tier or fidelity column, no last-evaluated-tick column (needed for reduced-rate ticking with interpolation, 100-arch line 49), no aggregate record type, and no link from an aggregate to its members for disaggregation.
- Step 3 (line 63) passes "current entity state" with no active-subset argument, although the behavior engine's tick accepts one (100-arch line 64).
- Line 35 names "region-aware entity management" as a decision that must not be precluded. No region concept appears in the document.
- Removal (line 70, "when appropriate") is unspecified. Compaction shifts indices and breaks any subset or index array a caller holds. Tombstones or a free list avoid that but leak into every mask.
- At capacity (line 84), the document does not say whether spawn fails or arrays reallocate. Reallocation invalidates any array reference the engine or serializer holds. "Fail explicitly" requires an answer.
- Ownership conflicts with the engine doc. Line 70 says the engine "does not manage the entity lifecycle," but 100-arch line 81 says the engine exposes "register/remove agents."

Required: add the cheap hooks now (tier and last-tick columns, an `active_indices` argument), choose compaction or free-list, define the capacity error, and state explicitly that aggregates are out of v1.

findings.title: A synchronous tick couples client I/O, logging, and overrun behavior
findings.description:
- **Blocking inside step 5.** Client pushes and log writes happen inside the tick (line 65). An `await` on a stalled client's send blocks the tick. Line 82 says this must not happen but names no mechanism. Per-client bounded queues with a sender task per client is the standard answer, and the document names neither. Log writes are synchronous disk I/O with unbounded latency.
- **Starvation under overrun.** Line 78 runs the tick synchronously on the event-loop thread. A tick that overruns also blocks every handshake, read, and keepalive for its full duration. "Continue at best effort" (line 88) therefore means the server stops answering when it is most loaded. The document does not analyze this failure mode.
- **Overrun semantics are unspecified.** It is unstated whether an overrun drops ticks, runs back-to-back catch-up ticks, or realigns to the next boundary. Catch-up couples simulated time to wall time, and the document uses "tick rate" for both.
- **Drift.** "Sleep for the remainder" (line 66) with relative sleeps accumulates drift. A fixed timestep needs absolute deadlines and a monotonic clock.
- **No clock abstraction.** Without an injectable clock the loop cannot be tested without real sleeps.

Required: decide where distribution and log writes run (behind queues), define overrun behavior, and specify the clock.

findings.title: Full per-tick snapshots break the bandwidth argument at the initial operating range
findings.description:
Line 108 calls egress "the second scaling wall" at 500K. The default described for ongoing clients, though, is full snapshots every tick (line 82 treats deltas as optional). Arithmetic at the document's own 10K–50K range, 20 tps, positions plus velocities in float32 (24 bytes per entity):

- 50K entities produce 1.2 MB per tick, or 24 MB/s per client.
- Ten observers, which the concept requires eventually, produce 240 MB/s from one process.

The document does not say whether clients receive 20 Hz updates or decimated ones, or how client-side interpolation handles it.

The connection snapshot (line 68) is unculled. At 50K entities it is 1.2 MB in one message, which exceeds the 1 MiB default receive limit of the `websockets` library if a Python consumer connects (the concept lists a raw telemetry client). At 500K it is about 12 MB. Slice 305's snapshot ("entity positions/velocities," 300-slices line 29) repeats this and contradicts the culling planned in slice 309.

Required: define the send rate, a per-client byte budget, and a chunked connect-time snapshot, or cull from v1.

findings.title: Scale claims are wrong on memory and unvalidated on throughput
findings.description:
- **Memory is wrong at the top tier.** "Memory is never the constraint" (line 92) holds for state only. The 24 MB figure at 500K matches 3D float64 position plus velocity (48 bytes per entity), but the document never states dimensionality. A NumPy-vectorized neighbor evaluation at 100 neighbors materializes 50M pairs at 500K. One (pairs × 3) float64 temporary is 1.2 GB, and the neighbor index array is 200–400 MB. That is roughly 50× the state. The top tier requires chunked evaluation with pre-allocated scratch, which conflicts with the "no dynamic allocation" requirement (100-arch line 99) and is not mentioned here.
- **The 10K–50K "comfortable" tier has no simulation benchmark.** The only evidence cited (100-arch line 56) is a 2,000-agent render prototype with no neighbor queries. At 50K entities with 100 neighbors, each tick evaluates 5M pairs (100M per second at 20 tps), with several array passes per pair. The document does not estimate whether that fits a 50 ms tick budget.
- **The GPU tier rests on an analogy.** Line 97 says "GPU particle simulations routinely handle 4M+ at 60fps — the physics is similar." Particle systems typically use simple per-particle forces, not 100-neighbor interactions. At 4M entities, 100 neighbors, and 20 tps, the workload is 8 billion neighbor interactions per second. The analogy does not support the claim.
- **No per-step budget.** Environment update (line 62, resource regeneration over the terrain grid), per-client culling and serialization, and logging all share the 50 ms budget with the engine. The document analyzes only the engine.

Required: state dimensionality and precision, replace "memory never the constraint" with a per-tier transient budget, benchmark the 10K and 50K points before the tier numbers stand, and allocate the tick budget across steps.

findings.title: The wire protocol and WebSocket stack are unspecified
findings.description:
- **Framing.** "Minimal framing (tick number, entity count, array layout descriptor)" (line 80) has no byte layout. Browser clients build `Float32Array` views on the buffer, and `new Float32Array(buffer, byteOffset)` throws a `RangeError` unless `byteOffset` is a multiple of 4. A header not padded to alignment breaks every client. A Float64 channel would need 8-byte alignment.
- **Endianness.** NumPy's `tobytes()` uses host byte order. The protocol must fix little-endian explicitly.
- **Descriptor placement.** A per-frame layout descriptor is avoidable overhead and belongs in a once-per-connection handshake. There is no protocol version and no message-type discriminator, so aggregate descriptors (line 108) and future admin commands (slice plan future item 4) cannot be added without breaking existing frames.
- **Library.** Line 53 says asyncio "well-serves" WebSockets, but asyncio has no WebSocket protocol. The library (`websockets`, `aiohttp`, Starlette) is unnamed. It determines backpressure, maximum message size, ping and keepalive, and close semantics, all of which this design depends on.
- **Float32 conversion.** The concept specifies Float32 for transfer and the engine may use float64 internally (100-arch line 95). Conversion is an O(N) copy per tick, which must be serialized once per tick and shared across clients and must fit the budget.
- **Downstream blocker.** The client layer (initiative 600) consumes this protocol (initiative plan lines 81–83) and cannot design against an unspecified contract.

Required: a protocol spec (header size, alignment, endianness, version, message type), a named library, and a serialize-once-per-tick rule.

findings.title: Environment ownership contradicts initiative 500, and the environment contract does not exist
findings.description:
- The Overview (line 19) says the server "owns... environment state."
- Anticipated Slices (line 122) lists "Environment layer foundation — terrain generation, resource placement, and the read-only query interface" as a 300 slice. The initiative plan places terrain, resources, and seasonal state under 500 (lines 51–52). The 300 entry in the same plan also claims "terrain and environmental data management" (line 42), so two initiatives claim terrain.
- Line 128 places "seasonal cycles, resource availability shifts, day/night" in 300. Slice 308 says the meaning of seasons is owned by 500 (300-slices line 35).
- Slice 304 depends on the 500 foundation (300-slices line 27), but this document's `dependsOn` (line 9) omits 500.
- The "read-only query interface" that step 3 depends on has no type or method list anywhere in the document set. Searches for environment and 500-band documents in this worktree returned nothing, so no document owns the contract.
- Line 72's "generated or loaded" is an unresolved either/or.

Required: move terrain, biome, and season semantics to 500 in this document, define the environment interface as the 300↔500 contract, and give the step-3 environment argument a type.

findings.title: The agent-to-environment write path is missing from the tick cycle
findings.description:
The tick cycle runs environment update, behavior evaluation, commit, and distribution. Nothing writes behavior results back into the environment. Swarm intelligence depends on stigmergy (100-arch line 77, "reinforced paths"), and slice 304 calls for "post-tick environment writes (e.g., stigmergic trail deposits)" (300-slices line 27). Meanwhile the engine is read-only over the environment (100-arch line 47: "It does not own or manage environmental data"). The data flow that carries trail deposits is not drawn. The document does not say which phase writes, what the next tick's environment update sees, or whether the writes are inside the transaction (see the first FAIL). "State flows outward" (line 43) covers clients only, so the agent-to-environment feedback loop is an implicit, unordered coupling.

Required: add an explicit deposit phase between commit and the next environment update, state whether it is transactional, and name the owner of the write.

findings.title: The engine's tick contract is described three ways and owned by an in-progress document
findings.description:
- Line 63 says the engine returns "updated positions and velocities."
- Line 64 says the server applies "the updated entity state" as canonical.
- Line 70 says the engine "operates on whatever entities the server provides."
- The behavior engine doc (100-arch lines 64–68) says the engine takes state, environment context, and an optional subset, and returns "the updated state array."
- Slice 303 says the server "commits the returned positions/velocities as canonical state" (300-slices line 25).

These are different return contracts: a full array, a partial set of columns, or a scatter back into canonical arrays for the active subset. Subset evaluation requires this to be settled. The initiative plan says 300 "cannot finalize its entity management design" until 100's agent state and tick signature are stable (lines 71–74). This document does not flag that dependency as blocking.

Required: write the tick signature once (inputs, outputs, and ownership of returned arrays), reference it from 100, and mark the dependency as blocking.

findings.title: Mutable state ownership and component boundaries are undefined
Operational logging, simulation recording, and metrics are conflated
Several load-bearing decisions are deferred or left implicit
findings.description:
- **Dimensionality.** The document never says whether the world is 2D or 3D. The numbers at lines 92 and 108 imply 3D (12-byte float32 positions).
- **Boundary semantics.** "Finite spatial bounds" (line 84) does not say whether edges clamp, reflect, wrap, or absorb. Each choice changes neighbor distance, the environment query domain, and the required behavior for out-of-bounds queries.
- **Precision.** Float64 versus float32 is left to the engine (100-arch line 95), but this document's numbers assume float64 state and float32 on the wire.
- **Configuration format.** Line 86 says "YAML or similar," but slice 300 is already complete and YAML-based (300-slices line 17).
- **Profile validation.** The engine interprets profiles (100-arch principle "Profile as data"). Nothing says who validates a profile before startup or how. "Validated before the server begins operation" cannot be met for profile semantics without an engine validation entry point.
- **Runtime configuration.** Line 90 lists "configuration changes" as replay inputs, but configuration is startup-only (line 47), and runtime parameter changes are future work.

Required: a short decisions table that settles each item.

findings.title: The WebSocket endpoint has no security posture
findings.description:
The document configures "network binding" (line 86) and streams full state to "any client" (line 68), but says nothing about default bind address, Origin validation, or authentication. Browsers do not apply the same-origin policy to WebSocket connections. Without an Origin check, any web page an observer visits can open a WebSocket to a local server and read the stream (cross-site WebSocket hijacking). Read-only observation is low-impact today, but the protocol is meant to leave room for admin commands (line 68; slice plan future item 4), which would make the same gap high-impact.

Required: default the bind address to loopback, validate Origin, and state the authentication posture for read-only clients and future command clients.

findings.title: The lifecycle promises persistence the plan defers, and v1 does not deliver a persistent world
findings.description:
- Line 45 requires the server to "persist state on shutdown," but persistence is deferred (300-slices future item 3, "State Persistence and World Save/Load").
- Line 57 says startup "creates initial entity populations from configured profiles," so every restart regenerates the world from configuration. The concept's central claim is a persistent world (concept line 36). This document calls the server "persistent" (line 19), but v1 is in-memory and regenerated from seeds.
- "Drain client connections gracefully" (line 45) has no defined behavior: close codes, deadline, or handling of an in-flight tick.
- Line 45 says error states are first-class, yet no state machine (starting, running, draining, stopped, failed) is given.

Required: state that v1 is non-persistent, move persist-on-shutdown to the future item, and define the lifecycle state machine.

findings.title: The scaling analysis is overweight for a foundation document and duplicates the behavior engine doc
findings.description:
About twenty lines (92–112) cover tiers from 1M to 4M+, multi-GPU partitioning, merge-event strategies, and cite astrophysics and wargaming. None of it decides anything; line 110 says "the architecture should not prescribe a solution." The initiative plan says 620 "need not be designed proactively" (lines 97–99), and the slice plan calls multi-resolution "premature for the foundation slice plan" (300-slices line 47). The same tier and aggregation material also appears in the behavior engine doc (100-arch lines 97–99).

Cut: move lines 92–112 into a 620 scale note. Keep the v1 constraints that matter: a subset-evaluable tick, tier and last-tick columns, IDs not tied to array indices, and the no-precluded-distribution rule (line 35). That removes roughly 80% of the section.

findings.title: Current State, Anticipated Slices, and cross-references disagree with the rest of the plan
findings.description:
- **Status.** Current State (line 51) says "No world server exists." The slice plan marks 300, 301, 302, and 303 complete (300-slices lines 17–25), while the initiative plan still says 300 is `not_started` (initiative plan line 44). Three documents give three answers to the most basic status question. I did not review implementation code, so this finding rests on the planning documents.
- **Duplicate slice list.** Anticipated Slices is a second, different list: seven items against the slice plan's ten plus future work. It merges 300 and 301 into one slice, omits serialization (306), temporal orchestration (308), and culling (309), and lists the environment foundation (500's scope) as a 300 slice. Delete the section and link to the slice plan (DRY).
- **Broken or stale links.** The frontmatter `dependsOn` (line 9) and Related Work (line 132) reference `001-concept.migratory`, but the file is `000-concept.migratory.md`. The behavior engine doc's Related Work (100-arch line 122) links to `200-arch.world-server-foundation.md`, which does not exist.

Required: fix the links, remove the duplicate slice list, update Current State from the slice plan, and reconcile the initiative plan.
